questions.question: What is the difference between DDL, DML, and DQL in SQL?
questions.title: DDL vs DML vs DQL in SQL
questions.direct_answer: SQL commands are grouped by purpose: **DDL** (Data Definition Language) defines structure — `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`; **DML** (Data Manipulation Language) changes data — `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`; **DQL** (Data Query Language) reads data — `SELECT`. DDL auto-commits; DML is transactional.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can categorize SQL commands and know DDL auto-commits while DML is transactional.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Lumping all SQL together and assuming everything can be rolled back.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention DCL (GRANT/REVOKE) and TCL (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) as the other two families.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **DDL** defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.
- **DML** changes data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
- **DQL** reads data: SELECT.
- **DDL auto-commits**; **DML is transactional** (COMMIT/ROLLBACK).
- **DCL** (GRANT/REVOKE) and **TCL** (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) are the other families.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: SQL commands are grouped into families based on what they do, and knowing the categories helps you reason about behaviour. DDL, data definition language, is about structure: CREATE to make a table, ALTER to change it, DROP to remove it, and TRUNCATE to empty it. DML, data manipulation language, is about the data inside tables: INSERT to add rows, UPDATE to change them, and DELETE to remove them. DQL, data query language, is about reading data, and that's essentially just SELECT, the R in CRUD. The behavioural difference that interviewers love is around transactions. DDL statements auto-commit, meaning their effect is permanent immediately and they typically commit any pending work, so you can't roll a CREATE or DROP back in most databases. DML, on the other hand, is transactional: you can wrap inserts, updates, and deletes in a transaction and either commit them or roll them back. There are two more families worth naming to show depth: DCL, data control language, which is GRANT and REVOKE for permissions, and TCL, transaction control language, which is COMMIT and ROLLBACK. So the quick mental map is DDL for structure, DML for data changes, DQL for reads, plus DCL and TCL for security and transactions.

sections.title: SQL Command Families
sections.content:
blue|DDL|~defines structure|CREATE ALTER DROP TRUNCATE|auto-commits|changes the schema
emerald|DML|~changes data|INSERT UPDATE DELETE|transactional|rollbackable
amber|DQL|~reads data|SELECT|no data change|the R in CRUD
rose|DCL / TCL|~security + txn|GRANT/REVOKE (DCL)|COMMIT/ROLLBACK (TCL)|round out the families

sections.title: One statement from each family
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming DDL is rollbackable**: in most databases DDL auto-commits and can't be undone.
- **Mixing DDL inside a transaction**: a DDL statement often commits the pending DML before it.
- **Calling SELECT 'DML'**: SELECT is DQL (it reads, doesn't change data).
- **Forgetting DCL/TCL exist**: GRANT/REVOKE and COMMIT/ROLLBACK are separate families.

questions.question: What are the main DDL commands and what does each do?
questions.title: DDL Commands in SQL — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
questions.direct_answer: The main **DDL** commands are **CREATE** (make a new table/index/database), **ALTER** (modify an existing object — add/drop/change columns), **DROP** (delete an object entirely), and **TRUNCATE** (remove all rows but keep the table). They define and change schema, and they auto-commit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the four core DDL commands and what each does.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing TRUNCATE (DDL, empties table) with DELETE (DML, removes rows).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note ALTER variants (ADD/DROP/MODIFY COLUMN) and that DDL auto-commits.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CREATE** makes a new object.
- **ALTER** modifies an existing object (add/drop/change columns).
- **DROP** deletes an object entirely.
- **TRUNCATE** empties a table but keeps its structure.
- **All DDL auto-commits** — effects are immediate.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The core DDL commands are CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and TRUNCATE, and together they define and evolve your database structure. CREATE makes a new object, most commonly a table, but also indexes, views, or databases. ALTER modifies an existing object; for a table that means adding a column, dropping a column, modifying a column's type, or adding and removing constraints, so ALTER is how your schema evolves over time. DROP deletes an object entirely, including both its structure and its data, so after dropping a table it no longer exists. TRUNCATE is the one people often confuse with DELETE: TRUNCATE is DDL and it removes all the rows from a table very quickly while keeping the table's structure intact, and it usually resets the auto-increment counter. DELETE, by contrast, is DML, can use a WHERE clause to remove specific rows, and is transactional. A key behaviour across all four DDL commands is that they auto-commit, so their effects are immediate and you generally can't roll them back; an accidental DROP usually means restoring from a backup. One production caution: ALTER on a very large table can rewrite or lock the table, so I plan those changes carefully.

emerald|ALTER|~modify object|ADD/DROP/MODIFY column|add constraints|evolves schema

sections.title: CREATE, ALTER, TRUNCATE, DROP
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(80));

ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(120);   -- add a column
ALTER TABLE customers MODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR(120); -- change a type

TRUNCATE TABLE customers;  -- remove all rows, keep the table
DROP TABLE customers;      -- remove the table entirely
```

*`CREATE`/`ALTER` shape the schema; `TRUNCATE` empties; `DROP` removes the object.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **TRUNCATE vs DELETE**: TRUNCATE is DDL and empties the whole table; DELETE is DML and can filter rows.
- **Expecting rollback**: DDL auto-commits — a wrong DROP usually needs a restore.
- **ALTER on huge tables**: some ALTERs rewrite/lock the table — plan for it in production.
- **DROP vs TRUNCATE confusion**: DROP removes the table; TRUNCATE keeps an empty one.

questions.question: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP in SQL?
questions.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **DELETE** (DML) removes rows, supports `WHERE`, is logged and rollbackable. **TRUNCATE** (DDL) empties the whole table fast, resets identity, and usually auto-commits. **DROP** (DDL) removes the table itself — structure and all. Same removal theme, very different scope and recoverability.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can rank DELETE/TRUNCATE/DROP by scope and recoverability.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating TRUNCATE like DELETE (expecting WHERE or rollback).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note DELETE is DML (transactional); TRUNCATE/DROP are DDL (auto-commit).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **DELETE** = DML, row-level, `WHERE`-able, rollbackable.
- **TRUNCATE** = DDL, fast full wipe, resets identity, auto-commits.
- **DROP** = DDL, removes the table and its structure.
- **TRUNCATE/DROP** generally can't be rolled back.
- **Pick by scope**: rows vs whole table vs the table object.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP all remove data, but they escalate in scope and differ in recoverability. DELETE is a DML command that removes rows. You can target specific rows with a WHERE clause, each removed row is logged, and because it's transactional you can roll it back inside a transaction. The trade-off is that row-by-row deletion is slower on big tables. TRUNCATE is a DDL command that empties the entire table in one fast operation, with no WHERE clause, and it resets the auto-increment counter. In most databases it auto-commits, so you generally can't undo it. DROP is also DDL, and it's the most drastic: it removes the table object itself, including its structure, columns, indexes, and constraints, not just the rows. So I choose based on scope. If I need to remove certain rows, or want the safety of rolling back, I use DELETE. If I want to wipe an entire table quickly, like resetting a staging table before a reload, I use TRUNCATE. If the table should genuinely cease to exist, I use DROP. And because TRUNCATE and DROP usually can't be rolled back, I make sure there's a backup before running them in production.

sections.title: DELETE / TRUNCATE / DROP
sections.content:
blue|DELETE|~rows, DML|WHERE allowed|logged + rollbackable|slower per row
emerald|TRUNCATE|~whole table, DDL|no WHERE, fast|resets identity|auto-commits
rose|DROP|~table itself, DDL|structure gone|indexes/constraints gone|auto-commits
amber|Recover|~know the risk|DELETE: undo in txn|TRUNCATE/DROP: restore from backup|

sections.title: Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | DELETE | TRUNCATE | DROP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Family | DML | DDL | DDL |
| WHERE | yes | no | n/a |
| Speed | slow | fast | fast |
| Rollback | yes (txn) | usually no | usually no |
| Table remains | yes | yes (empty) | no |

sections.title: DELETE: selective and reversible
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM logs WHERE created < '2025-01-01';  -- only old rows
ROLLBACK;  -- undone: DELETE is transactional
```

sections.title: TRUNCATE / DROP: wholesale and structural
sections.content:
```sql
TRUNCATE TABLE logs;   -- empties fast, resets identity, auto-commits
DROP TABLE logs;       -- removes the table entirely
```

*DELETE for specific, recoverable removal; TRUNCATE to wipe fast; DROP to delete the table.*

sections.title: When to Use Which
sections.content: Use **DELETE** to remove *specific* rows or when you need transactional safety. Use **TRUNCATE** to clear an entire table quickly (staging/reload) with no WHERE or rollback needed. Use **DROP** when the table should no longer exist at all.

questions.question: What are DML commands in SQL and how are they used?
questions.title: DML Commands in SQL — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
questions.direct_answer: **DML** (Data Manipulation Language) changes the data inside tables: **INSERT** adds rows, **UPDATE** modifies existing rows, **DELETE** removes rows. DML is **transactional** — you can wrap statements in a transaction and `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. Always use a `WHERE` with UPDATE/DELETE to avoid changing every row.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the DML commands and that they're transactional.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE and changing every row.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention wrapping multi-statement DML in a transaction for atomicity.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **DML** = INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — changes table data.
- **Transactional**: COMMIT to keep, ROLLBACK to undo.
- **Always use WHERE** with UPDATE/DELETE.
- **Group multi-step changes** in a transaction for atomicity.
- **Batch** very large modifications to avoid long locks.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: DML, data manipulation language, is how you change the actual data inside your tables, and it has three commands. INSERT adds new rows, either with explicit VALUES or by selecting from another query. UPDATE modifies values in existing rows using a SET clause. And DELETE removes rows. The most important habit with UPDATE and DELETE is to always include a WHERE clause, because if you forget it, UPDATE changes every row in the table and DELETE removes every row, which is one of the classic ways people cause a production disaster. The other defining property of DML is that it's transactional. You can wrap a sequence of DML statements in a transaction with BEGIN and then either COMMIT to make them all permanent or ROLLBACK to undo them all. This is what keeps multi-step changes atomic; for example, transferring money by subtracting from one account and adding to another should either both happen or neither, and a transaction guarantees that. A couple more practical points: changes aren't durable until they're committed, and client auto-commit settings vary, so I'm explicit; and for very large updates or deletes I batch the work to avoid holding long locks and bloating the transaction log.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
SQL commands are grouped by purpose: **DDL** (Data Definition Language) defines structure — `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`; **DML** (Data Manipulation Language) changes data — `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`; **DQL** (Data Query Language) reads data — `SELECT`.

DDL auto-commits; DML is transactional.

**DML** (Data Manipulation Language) changes the data inside tables: **INSERT** adds rows, **UPDATE** modifies existing rows, **DELETE** removes rows. DML is **transactional** — you can wrap statements in a transaction and `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. Always use a `WHERE` with UPDATE/DELETE to avoid changing every row.

Lumping all SQL together and assuming everything can be rolled back.

sections.title: DML at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|INSERT|~add rows|INSERT INTO ... VALUES|or INSERT ... SELECT|new data
blue|UPDATE|~modify rows|SET col = value|needs WHERE!|changes existing data
rose|DELETE|~remove rows|with WHERE|else wipes table|removes data
amber|Transactional|~atomic changes|BEGIN ... COMMIT|or ROLLBACK|all-or-nothing

sections.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE in a transaction
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO accounts (id, balance) VALUES (1, 1000);
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;  -- WHERE!
DELETE FROM accounts WHERE balance < 0;                    -- WHERE!
COMMIT;   -- all three changes become permanent together
```

*Wrapping the statements makes them atomic — ROLLBACK would undo all three.*

sections.title: DELETE without WHERE — wipes every row
sections.content:
```sql
-- DANGER: no WHERE clause
DELETE FROM users;
-- Removes EVERY row in users, not just the one you meant.
-- UPDATE users SET status = 'inactive';  -- same trap: sets every row
```

*The query runs fine and reports thousands of rows affected — that's the moment a fresher realizes the WHERE was missing.*

sections.title: Scoped DELETE inside a transaction — safe and reversible
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 42;   -- targets ONE row
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE id = 42;  -- verify before committing
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK if the count looks wrong
```

*Add the WHERE first, run inside a transaction, and check the result before COMMIT — a wrong DELETE can still be rolled back.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE**: changes or deletes every row — a classic disaster.
- **Forgetting to COMMIT**: changes aren't durable until committed (auto-commit varies by client).
- **Partial multi-step changes**: not using a transaction can leave data half-updated.
- **Mass updates without batching**: huge UPDATE/DELETE can lock rows and bloat logs.

questions.question: What is TCL in SQL and why is it important?
questions.title: TCL in SQL — COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
questions.direct_answer: **TCL** (Transaction Control Language) manages transactions: **COMMIT** makes changes permanent, **ROLLBACK** undoes them, and **SAVEPOINT** marks a point to partially roll back to. TCL gives DML its **atomicity** — a group of changes succeeds together or not at all.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know TCL commands and that they control DML transactions (ACID atomicity).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that DDL auto-commits, so TCL can't undo a DROP/CREATE.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie TCL to ACID and explain SAVEPOINT for partial rollback.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **TCL** = COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.
- **COMMIT** makes changes permanent; **ROLLBACK** undoes them.
- **SAVEPOINT** allows partial rollback within a transaction.
- **TCL provides atomicity** — the A in ACID.
- **DDL auto-commits**, so TCL can't undo it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: TCL, transaction control language, is the set of commands that manage transactions, and a transaction is the unit that makes a group of changes atomic. There are three main commands. COMMIT makes all the changes in the current transaction permanent and ends the transaction. ROLLBACK discards the changes and returns the data to how it was at the start of the transaction. And SAVEPOINT sets a named marker inside a transaction, so you can roll back just to that point without throwing away everything you've done. TCL is what delivers the A in ACID, atomicity, which means a set of related changes either all succeed or all fail together. The textbook example is a money transfer: you debit one account and credit another, and you wrap both in a transaction so that if the credit fails, the debit is rolled back too and money is never lost. SAVEPOINT is useful for more granular control, letting you undo part of a transaction while keeping earlier work. The important caveat to mention is that DDL auto-commits, so TCL can't help you there; you cannot roll back a DROP or a CREATE with ROLLBACK. And practically, I keep transactions short, because holding locks for a long time blocks other users.

**TCL** (Transaction Control Language) manages transactions: **COMMIT** makes changes permanent, **ROLLBACK** undoes them, and **SAVEPOINT** marks a point to partially roll back to. TCL gives DML its **atomicity** — a group of changes succeeds together or not at all.

sections.content:
emerald|COMMIT|~make permanent|ends transaction|changes durable|
rose|ROLLBACK|~undo changes|back to start|or to a SAVEPOINT|
blue|SAVEPOINT|~partial marker|roll back part|keep earlier work|nested control
amber|Why|~ACID atomicity|all-or-nothing|protects multi-step DML|DDL auto-commits anyway

sections.title: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting to ROLLBACK DDL**: DDL auto-commits — you can't undo a DROP/ALTER with ROLLBACK.
- **Forgetting to COMMIT**: work stays uncommitted (and may be lost on disconnect).
- **Long-running transactions**: holding locks too long blocks other users.
- **Misusing SAVEPOINT**: it's for partial undo within one transaction, not a substitute for COMMIT.

questions.question: Why do DDL statements auto-commit in most databases?
questions.title: Why DDL Statements Auto-Commit in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **DDL statements auto-commit** because they change the database's **structure (schema)**, which can't sit half-applied inside a transaction. Most databases implicitly commit any pending work before and after a DDL statement, so a `CREATE`/`ALTER`/`DROP` is permanent immediately and ends the current transaction.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why DDL auto-commits and its impact on open transactions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming a DDL inside a transaction can be rolled back with the DML around it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note this is engine-dependent (some DBs support transactional DDL) and that DDL commits pending DML.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **DDL auto-commits** via an implicit COMMIT in most engines.
- **It commits pending DML** before running.
- **`CREATE`/`ALTER`/`DROP`** are permanent immediately.
- **Can't be rolled back** in MySQL/Oracle.
- **Engine-dependent**: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: DDL statements auto-commit because they change the database's structure, the schema, and a schema change can't sensibly sit half-applied inside a transaction. In most engines like MySQL and Oracle, running a DDL statement triggers an implicit commit: the database first commits any pending transaction you have open, then runs the DDL, then commits that too and starts a fresh transaction. The practical consequences are twofold. First, a CREATE, ALTER, or DROP is permanent the moment it runs and you can't roll it back, so an accidental DROP usually means restoring from a backup. Second, and this surprises a lot of people, a DDL statement will silently commit the DML you ran just before it. So if you insert some rows and then create a table in the same session, those inserts are now committed and a later ROLLBACK won't undo them. The underlying reason is that schema changes are hard to express as reversible row-level operations, and other sessions need a consistent view of the table structure, so the engine doesn't keep them pending. The one nuance worth mentioning is that this is engine-dependent: PostgreSQL actually supports transactional DDL, where you can roll back a CREATE or ALTER, whereas MySQL and Oracle do not. So I always check the database before assuming.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
SQL commands are grouped by purpose: **DDL** (Data Definition Language) defines structure — `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`; **DML** (Data Manipulation Language) changes data — `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`; **DQL** (Data Query Language) reads data — `SELECT`.

DDL auto-commits; DML is transactional.

**DDL statements auto-commit** because they change the database's **structure (schema)**, which can't sit half-applied inside a transaction. Most databases implicitly commit any pending work before and after a DDL statement, so a `CREATE`/`ALTER`/`DROP` is permanent immediately and ends the current transaction.

Lumping all SQL together and assuming everything can be rolled back.

sections.title: DDL Auto-Commit at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What happens|~implicit COMMIT|commits pending DML first|then runs DDL|then commits DDL
rose|Consequence|~no rollback|CREATE/ALTER/DROP permanent|ends your transaction|backup before risky DDL
amber|Why|~schema not row-level|hard to reverse cleanly|other sessions need consistency|
emerald|Engine note|~not universal|MySQL/Oracle auto-commit|PostgreSQL transactional DDL|verify your DB

sections.title: DDL commits the DML around it
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO logs VALUES (1, 'start');   -- pending DML

CREATE TABLE temp_report (id INT);       -- DDL: implicit COMMIT here!
-- the INSERT above is now COMMITTED and can no longer be rolled back

ROLLBACK;   -- too late for the INSERT; only affects work AFTER the DDL
```

*In MySQL/Oracle the DDL silently commits the earlier INSERT — a common surprise.*

sections.title: Expecting ROLLBACK to undo a DDL (MySQL)
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, total) VALUES (1, 50);
DROP TABLE old_orders;   -- DDL: implicit COMMIT — the INSERT is now permanent
ROLLBACK;                -- does NOT bring old_orders back, and the INSERT stays
```

*A fresher assumes the whole block is one transaction. In MySQL the DROP already committed everything before it.*

sections.title: Keep DDL out of the DML transaction
sections.content:
```sql
-- Finish (or roll back) the data transaction FIRST
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, total) VALUES (1, 50);
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK — decided cleanly, on its own

-- Then run schema changes separately, with a backup ready
DROP TABLE old_orders;   -- auto-commits, as expected
```

*Separate the two: settle DML in its own transaction, then run DDL on its own — no surprise commits.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting rollback of DDL**: a wrong DROP/ALTER usually needs a restore.
- **Mixing DDL into a DML transaction**: the DDL commits your pending DML unexpectedly.
- **Assuming all engines behave alike**: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL; MySQL/Oracle don't.
- **No backup before risky schema changes**: there's no ROLLBACK to save you.
